title: Later Zhou
capsule: Later Zhou was the last and most capable of the Five Dynasties that governed northern China between 907 and 960, founded by Guo Wei in 951 after he deposed the Later Han. Emperor Shizong (Chai Rong, r. 954–959) undertook systematic military and administrative reforms — streamlining the army, standardizing coinage, reducing monastic landholdings, and launching three northern campaigns that recovered the Huai River basin from the Southern Tang — which laid the institutional groundwork that the Song dynasty would build upon. Shizong died in 959 before completing his reunification campaigns; his successor, the child emperor Gong Di, was dethroned in 960 when general Zhao Kuangyin staged the Chenqiao Mutiny and founded the Song dynasty.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Later Zhou's territorial extent in northern China is well-attested by the standard Chinese dynastic histories (Xin Wudai Shi, Jiu Wudai Shi); exact boundaries of the contested Huai River frontier with southern kingdoms involve some scholarly interpolation. Note: the dataset's from-year of -750 reflects a broader 'Zhou' periodization grouping rather than the historically distinct Later Zhou founded in 951.
